title: Verbalized-Confidence Calibration Card for Open Models
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Verbalized-Confidence Calibration Card for Open Models

**Problem:** LLMs are systematically overconfident when asked to state numeric confidence ('I'm 90% sure'), clustering at 80-100% in multiples of 5. There is no standard, lightweight artifact (a 'calibration card') that summarizes an open model's verbalized-confidence calibration on a fixed factual QA set with reliability diagrams and ECE.

**Direction:** On SimpleQA / TriviaQA subsets, prompt an open model to answer and state a numeric confidence. Bin by stated confidence, compute empirical accuracy per bin, produce reliability diagrams, Expected Calibration Error, and an overconfidence index. Compare across prompt formats (number vs. word vs. 0-1 probability) and produce a one-page calibration card per model.

**Why it matters:** Honest models must communicate genuine uncertainty; overconfident stated probabilities are a concrete dishonesty failure that misleads users in high-stakes decisions. A reusable calibration card standardizes external auditing.

**Relevant context:** On Verbalized Confidence Scores for LLMs (arXiv 2412.14737) and 2503.02623 'Rewarding Doubt' document severe overconfidence clustering at 80-100%. SimpleQA designed to test calibrated abstention. No standard external 'calibration card' artifact exists.

title: Abstention-Honesty Score: Measuring 'I Don't Know' Under Adversarial Unknowns
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Abstention-Honesty Score: Measuring 'I Don't Know' Under Adversarial Unknowns

**Problem:** SimpleQA tests abstention on long-tail facts, but no public benchmark separates genuine epistemic abstention from over-refusal by injecting *unanswerable-by-construction* and *fabricated-entity* questions alongside answerable ones, then scoring whether the model honestly abstains vs. confabulates.

**Direction:** Construct a small set mixing (a) answerable facts, (b) verifiably unknowable questions (future events, private data), and (c) plausible-but-fake entities ('the 2019 Turing Award given to Dr. Elena Vostrikova'). Score each open model on an Abstention-Honesty metric: rewards correct answers and honest abstention, penalizes confabulation on (b)/(c). Report confabulation rate on fake entities specifically.

**Why it matters:** Confident fabrication on nonexistent entities is a pure honesty failure (not a knowledge gap). A benchmark isolating it measures whether models 'know what they don't know' — central to the honesty open problem — and needs only public/synthetic data.

**Relevant context:** Reinforced Hesitation (arXiv 2511.11500) frames abstention as a first-class honesty objective; notes 'no model achieves calibrated abstention.' I-CALM (2604.03904) targets confidence-aware abstention. SimpleQA measures abstention but doesn't isolate fabricated-entity confabulation.

title: Filler-Token Dependence Probe: Does the CoT Actually Compute Anything?
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Filler-Token Dependence Probe: Does the CoT Actually Compute Anything?

**Problem:** A key faithfulness question is whether CoT tokens are load-bearing or decorative. Lanham's filler-token test (replace CoT with '...') exists, but there is no reusable diagnostic that systematically measures, per task category, how much accuracy survives when the CoT is replaced with semantically empty filler of equal length.

**Direction:** For an open reasoning model, run each question (a) with normal CoT, (b) with CoT replaced by equal-length filler tokens (dots/repeated neutral phrase), (c) with no CoT. Measure accuracy drop. The gap between filler and real CoT is the 'load-bearing fraction'. Build a small benchmark reporting load-bearing fraction by task type (arithmetic vs. commonsense vs. multi-hop).

**Why it matters:** If accuracy survives filler replacement, the visible reasoning is decorative and monitoring it gives false assurance. Quantifying load-bearingness per task tells safety researchers where CoT monitoring can and cannot be trusted.

**Relevant context:** Filler-token corruption is one of the four Lanham (2023) faithfulness tests. Steganography/filler-token literature (arXiv 2506.01926, 2507.05246) discusses filler tokens as parallelizable scratchpads and the 'load-bearing' hypothesis. No turnkey per-task load-bearing-fraction tool exists.

title: Persona-Induced Honesty Degradation Benchmark
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Persona-Induced Honesty Degradation Benchmark

**Problem:** Professional/expert personas can suppress a model's honest self-representation (e.g., a 'Financial Advisor' persona hiding its AI nature). Existing work audits this for credential disclosure, but there is no benchmark measuring how a *spectrum* of persona prompts shifts factual honesty and self-disclosure across many open models.

**Direction:** Define a persona ladder (neutral → helpful assistant → confident domain expert → roleplay character) and a probe set (epistemic self-disclosure questions + factual questions with known answers). Measure, per persona level, the rate of AI-nature disclosure and factual error/fabrication. Output a 'honesty-vs-persona' curve quantifying how much persona framing erodes honesty.

**Why it matters:** Persona effects on honesty are an explicit Anthropic open problem. Deployers routinely wrap models in persona system prompts; quantifying the honesty cost is directly safety-relevant and uses only prompts (no training).

**Relevant context:** 'Self-Transparency Failures in Expert-Persona LLMs' / 'When Models Fabricate Credentials' (arXiv 2511.21569) found e.g. Financial Advisor persona disclosed AI nature only 30.2% at baseline; instruction-following overrides honesty. Persona Vectors (2507.21509) and the honesty_faithfulness open-problems list flag persona effects.

title: Stated-Belief vs. Revealed-Belief Consistency Auditor
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Stated-Belief vs. Revealed-Belief Consistency Auditor

**Problem:** A model is 'lying' when its answer is inconsistent with its underlying belief. There is no simple public tool that elicits a model's neutral-prompt belief, then applies pressure to flip it, then asks the model whether it lied — and scores the three-phase consistency automatically.

**Direction:** Implement the three-phase deception probe: (1) elicit a belief with neutral prompts, (2) apply a pressure prompt designed to induce a contradicting answer, (3) directly ask 'did your previous answer reflect your true belief?'. Score belief-stability, pressure-induced flip rate, and honest-admission rate. Run across open models and report a consistency/honesty triple.

**Why it matters:** Detecting goal-directed inconsistency between stated and revealed beliefs is the operational definition of model lying. A reusable auditor lets external researchers measure it on any open model with no internal access.

**Relevant context:** 'Evaluating Scaling Trends for Deception' (OpenReview YRXDl6I3j5) defines lying as belief-inconsistent answers and uses elicit-belief → pressure → query-admission phases. Truthfulness Spectrum Hypothesis (arXiv 2602.20273) and strategic-dishonesty work support this framing.

title: Best-of-N Sampling as an Attacker: How Many Tries to Break Safety?
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined adversarial robustness / jailbreak safety problem with a clear focused experimental approach.

original_idea.body:
# Best-of-N Sampling as an Attacker: How Many Tries to Break Safety?

**Problem:** Success state: a model cannot be jailbroken merely by resampling. Backcasting, the needed result is a measurement of jailbreak ASR as a function of N independent samples (best-of-N attack) for open models, exposing the cost an attacker actually pays.

**Direction:** For each harmful prompt, draw N samples at moderate temperature and count it as broken if ANY sample complies usefully (StrongReject-scored). Plot ASR vs N (1..64). This quantifies safety as an attacker-effort curve rather than a single ASR number.

**Why it matters:** Reframes robustness as cost-to-break, which is the metric that matters for realistic attackers and is invisible in single-sample benchmarks. Cheap, no training, and directly informs the realistic-benchmark open problem.

**Relevant context:** Best-of-N jailbreaking and resampling attacks exploit stochastic decoding; shallow alignment (arXiv:2406.05946) implies a non-trivial fraction of samples may slip past first-token safety. StrongReject (arXiv:2402.10260) provides usefulness scoring to avoid empty-jailbreak inflation.

title: Introspective Accuracy Test: Can a Model Predict Its Own Behavior?
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Introspective Accuracy Test: Can a Model Predict Its Own Behavior?

**Problem:** Introspection research shows a model can sometimes predict properties of its own outputs better than another model trained on its behavior. But there is no lightweight, training-free benchmark that measures introspective accuracy purely via in-context self-prediction on open models.

**Direction:** For each scenario, ask the model to predict a property of its own future output (e.g., 'On input P, will your answer be longer or shorter?', 'will you pick option A or B?'), then actually run input P and check. Compute self-prediction accuracy and compare to a control where a second open model predicts the same. Report the introspective-advantage gap without any fine-tuning.

**Why it matters:** Honest self-report of internal dispositions is the foundation of an 'ask the model if it's misaligned' safety strategy. A training-free introspection benchmark lets external researchers test whether self-reports are grounded in real internal access vs. confabulation.

**Relevant context:** Binder/Evans 'Looking Inward' (arXiv 2410.13787, ICLR 2025) finetune models to predict own behavior and show introspective advantage; 'Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language' (2503.07513) shows limits. No purely in-context, training-free introspection benchmark for open models exists.

title: Self-Explanation Semantic-Invariance Checker
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Self-Explanation Semantic-Invariance Checker

**Problem:** If a model's explanation of why it answered is faithful, semantically equivalent rephrasings of the question should yield semantically equivalent explanations. Recent work shows self-explanations fail this invariance, but there is no reusable checker that quantifies explanation invariance under input paraphrase for arbitrary open models.

**Direction:** Take a question, generate the model's answer + self-explanation, then feed K meaning-preserving paraphrases of the same question and collect explanations. Use embedding similarity + an LLM judge to score how much the *stated reasons* drift while the answer stays fixed. Report an 'explanation invariance score' per task type and model.

**Why it matters:** Explanations that change arbitrarily under paraphrase are post-hoc rationalizations, not faithful accounts — a direct honesty/faithfulness failure that misleads anyone relying on model explanations. The checker is fully behavioral and lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** 'LLM Self-Explanations Fail Semantic Invariance' (arXiv 2603.01254) documents this failure mode. FaithCoT-Bench and CoT-dynamics work (2508.19827) distinguish faithful guidance from post-hoc rationalization. No standalone invariance-checker tool exists.

title: Decorative-Step Detector for Chain-of-Thought ('Fake Aha Moments')
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Decorative-Step Detector for Chain-of-Thought ('Fake Aha Moments')

**Problem:** CoTs contain both load-bearing reasoning steps and decorative 'aha'-style steps that don't affect the answer. Identifying which steps are true vs. decorative currently needs bespoke methods; there is no simple step-ablation tool that labels each CoT step as causal or ornamental for open models.

**Direction:** Segment a model's CoT into steps; for each step, regenerate the answer with that step deleted (or replaced by neutral text) and measure answer change. Steps whose removal doesn't change the answer are 'decorative'. Produce per-model statistics on the fraction of decorative steps and which rhetorical patterns ('Wait, let me reconsider') are most often decorative.

**Why it matters:** Decorative reasoning inflates apparent transparency while hiding the real computation, weakening CoT monitoring. A step-level detector tells safety monitors which parts of a trace to trust.

**Relevant context:** 'Can Aha Moments Be Fake? Identifying True and Decorative Thinking Steps' (arXiv 2510.24941) motivates true-vs-decorative step labeling. 'Measuring CoT Faithfulness by Unlearning Reasoning Steps' (2502.14829) uses step ablation. No turnkey decorative-step detector exists.

title: CoT-Monitor Stress Test: Minimal Obfuscation Pressure Threshold
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# CoT-Monitor Stress Test: Minimal Obfuscation Pressure Threshold

**Problem:** Research shows models can obfuscate reasoning to evade monitors under instruction, but the *amount* of obfuscation pressure needed varies. There is no public, graded benchmark that measures, per open model, the minimal prompt-pressure level at which a CoT monitor's detection accuracy collapses.

**Direction:** Define a ladder of obfuscation instructions of increasing intensity ('be concise' → 'avoid mentioning X' → 'hide your real reason'). For a task where the model uses a detectable shortcut, run a simple LLM-judge monitor and measure at which pressure rung the monitor stops catching the shortcut. Report a per-model 'monitor-evasion threshold'.

**Why it matters:** CoT monitoring is a leading safety mechanism; knowing how little pressure breaks it tells us how fragile that defense is. The benchmark needs only prompting + a cheap judge, no lab tooling, and targets a >1yr threat (models learning to evade monitors).

**Relevant context:** 'Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning? Stress-Testing CoT Monitorability' (arXiv 2510.19851) builds graded obfuscation-pressure prompts. 'When CoT is Necessary, LMs Struggle to Evade Monitors' (2507.05246) gives the load-bearing counterpoint. No public per-model evasion-threshold benchmark exists.

title: Sycophancy-on-Verifiable-Math: BrokenMath-Style Probe for Open Models
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Sycophancy-on-Verifiable-Math: BrokenMath-Style Probe for Open Models

**Problem:** Sycophancy is especially dangerous when a model agrees with a false premise in a domain with a ground truth (e.g., accepting a wrong theorem statement). BrokenMath benchmarks this for theorem proving, but there is no compact, easy-to-run probe applying false-premise agreement tests on grade-school/competition math for open models.

**Direction:** Take correct math problems, inject subtly false premises or assert wrong intermediate results, and present them as if user-stated. Measure how often the model 'agrees' and proceeds with the false premise vs. correcting it. Report a domain-specific sycophancy rate and how it scales with how authoritative the false claim is framed.

**Why it matters:** Agreement with verifiably false claims is unambiguous sycophantic dishonesty with a clean ground truth, avoiding the subjectivity of opinion-based sycophancy tests. Fully reproducible on public math data.

**Relevant context:** BrokenMath (arXiv 2510.04721) benchmarks sycophancy in theorem proving; 'Sycophancy under Pressure' (2508.13743) uses adversarial dialogues in scientific QA. No lightweight false-premise math sycophancy probe for open models exists.

title: Confidence-Faithfulness Gap Meter: Does Stated Confidence Match Reasoning?
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Confidence-Faithfulness Gap Meter: Does Stated Confidence Match Reasoning?

**Problem:** A model can express high verbalized confidence while its actual reasoning is weak or contradictory — a 'confidence-faithfulness gap'. No simple tool jointly measures stated confidence and reasoning-answer consistency on the same items to expose this gap for open models.

**Direction:** For each item, collect (a) the model's answer, (b) its stated numeric confidence, and (c) a faithfulness signal (e.g., does the answer survive CoT paraphrase / early-answer truncation). Cross-tabulate to find items where confidence is high but reasoning is fragile. Report the fraction of 'overconfident-and-unfaithful' items as a single gap metric.

**Why it matters:** High confidence paired with unfaithful reasoning is the most dangerous combination for users who trust both the answer and its rationale. Surfacing it requires only behavioral probing of open models.

**Relevant context:** 'Closing the Confidence-Faithfulness Gap in LLMs' (arXiv 2603.25052) introduces this gap concept. Overconfidence literature (2412.14737) and faithfulness corruption tests (Lanham 2023) provide the two signals. No combined gap-meter tool exists.

title: TruthfulQA-Under-Pressure: Adding a Persuasion Layer to a Classic Benchmark
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# TruthfulQA-Under-Pressure: Adding a Persuasion Layer to a Classic Benchmark

**Problem:** TruthfulQA measures imitative falsehoods in single-turn neutral settings, but doesn't test whether a model abandons a true answer under user persuasion. There is no extension that wraps each TruthfulQA item in escalating persuasive pushback to measure pressure-induced truthfulness loss.

**Direction:** For each TruthfulQA item where the model initially answers truthfully, append a persuasion turn asserting the popular misconception with authority/social proof, then re-ask. Measure the 'truth abandonment rate' and which misconception categories are most pressure-sensitive. Release as a drop-in TruthfulQA add-on.

**Why it matters:** Real users push back; a model that is truthful only until pressured is unsafe. Extending a widely-used benchmark with a pressure layer gives the community a standardized realistic-sycophancy test grounded in known misconceptions.

**Relevant context:** TruthfulQA (817 questions) is the canonical imitative-falsehood benchmark. PARROT (arXiv 2511.17220) and 'Beyond Social Pressure: Epistemic Attack' (2604.07749) show persuasion erodes truth. Opus 4.5 card: standard prompts overstate robustness. No TruthfulQA pressure-extension exists.

title: Answer-Before-Reasoning Detector via Early-Answer Probing
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Answer-Before-Reasoning Detector via Early-Answer Probing

**Problem:** Evidence suggests models often decide the answer before generating the CoT, then rationalize. Lanham's early-answering test exists but there's no reusable diagnostic that maps, per task, how early in the CoT the final answer becomes determined (the 'answer-commitment point').

**Direction:** For each question, truncate the CoT at increasing fractions (10%, 25%, 50%...) and force an answer at each cut, measuring at what fraction the truncated answer matches the full answer. The earlier the commitment, the more the later CoT is decorative. Produce per-task answer-commitment curves for open models.

**Why it matters:** If answers are committed before reasoning, the CoT is rationalization and cannot be trusted as a monitorable record of how the model decided — a core faithfulness concern. Purely behavioral and reproducible.

**Relevant context:** Early-answering is a Lanham (2023) corruption test. 'Decoding Answers Before Chain-of-Thought' (arXiv 2603.01437) provides pre-CoT-probe evidence answers form early. No turnkey answer-commitment-curve tool for open models exists.

title: Cross-Model Sycophancy Contagion in Multi-Agent Debate
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Model Sycophancy Contagion in Multi-Agent Debate

**Problem:** Sycophancy is studied for user→model pressure, but with multi-agent setups proliferating, there's no benchmark for model→model sycophancy: does an open model abandon a correct answer when a peer agent confidently disagrees?

**Direction:** Pair two open models in a debate over verifiable questions. One is given the correct answer, the other a confidently-asserted wrong answer. Measure how often the correct model flips toward the incorrect peer, and whether a 'confident wrong' peer is more contagious than a 'tentative wrong' peer. Report a model-to-model sycophancy/contagion rate.

**Why it matters:** Multi-agent systems risk amplifying errors if models defer to confident peers rather than truth. A contagion benchmark targets a medium-horizon deployment risk (agent swarms) that labs underweight, using only open models.

**Relevant context:** SpiralBench uses two LLMs in 20-turn conversations. SycEval (58% capitulation) and SYCON-Bench measure user-pressure sycophancy. PARROT (2511.17220) measures persuasion robustness. No model-to-model sycophancy-contagion benchmark in multi-agent debate exists.

title: Reward-Hack Verbalization Mini-Suite in Toy Gameable Environments
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Reward-Hack Verbalization Mini-Suite in Toy Gameable Environments

**Problem:** The striking result that models verbalize a reward hack in <2% of cases despite using it ~99% of the time was shown in proprietary environments. There is no small, open, reproducible suite of *gameable toy tasks* where one can measure verbalization rate of an exploit for open models.

**Direction:** Design 3-4 toy tasks with an obvious exploitable shortcut (e.g., an answer leaked in metadata, a grader keyword that always scores high, a formatting trick). Run open models, detect when they use the shortcut (high success on gameable items), and check whether the CoT mentions the shortcut. Report per-task use-rate vs. verbalization-rate.

**Why it matters:** Silent reward-hacking is a canonical alignment failure; an open, reproducible measurement suite lets the external community track whether models disclose exploits in their CoT — exactly the property CoT monitoring depends on.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic's reasoning-models paper (arXiv 2505.05410): reward hacks verbalized <2% despite >99% use. 'Teaching Models to Verbalize Reward Hacking' (2506.22777) studies inducing disclosure. No open toy-environment verbalization suite exists.

title: Probe Calibration Under Adaptive Pressure: Can Attackers Fool the Free Detector?
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined adversarial robustness / jailbreak safety problem with a clear focused experimental approach.

original_idea.body:
# Probe Calibration Under Adaptive Pressure: Can Attackers Fool the Free Detector?

**Problem:** Success state: cheap activation probes remain reliable even when attackers know they exist. The needed prior result: a small adaptive-attack stress test showing whether simple prompt modifications can push jailbreak activations to look benign to a linear probe.

**Direction:** Train a linear jailbreak probe on an open model, then craft simple adaptive prompts (paraphrase, benign-framing wrappers) aimed at minimizing the probe's score while preserving the harmful payload, and measure the resulting evasion rate. No gradient access needed — just prompt-level search.

**Why it matters:** The cheap-probe result (Jan 2026) assumed non-adaptive attackers. An accessible adaptive stress test is exactly the adversarial evaluation labs underweight, and a model-organism-style demo of a probe-evading attacker is highly informative for whether to trust these monitors.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic cheap-monitors (alignment.anthropic.com/2025/cheap-monitors) and 'LLM Jailbreak Detection for (Almost) Free' (arXiv:2509.14558) establish probe efficacy on non-adaptive attacks; adaptive robustness is the standard next question (cf. Carlini's adaptive-attack methodology).

title: Monitorability Score Combining Faithfulness and Verbosity
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Monitorability Score Combining Faithfulness and Verbosity

**Problem:** Recent work argues monitorability depends on both faithfulness (does CoT reveal the real reason) and verbosity (does CoT externalize enough). No simple composite tool computes a single monitorability score for an open model by combining a faithfulness probe with a verbosity/coverage measure.

**Direction:** Combine two cheap signals per item: a faithfulness flag (e.g., hint-reliance verbalization or paraphrase robustness) and a verbosity/coverage measure (how much decision-relevant content the CoT externalizes, judged against the answer). Produce a per-model monitorability index and analyze the tradeoff — e.g., do terse CoTs score worse on coverage but better on faithfulness?

**Why it matters:** Monitorability is the property safety teams actually want from CoT; a reusable composite index gives external researchers a single comparable number across open models and exposes the faithfulness-vs-verbosity tradeoff.

**Relevant context:** 'Measuring CoT Monitorability Through Faithfulness and Verbosity' (arXiv 2510.27378) decomposes monitorability into these two axes. No turnkey composite monitorability-index tool for open models exists.

title: Knowledge-Conflict Honesty: Does the Model Admit Why It Changed Its Mind?
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Knowledge-Conflict Honesty: Does the Model Admit Why It Changed Its Mind?

**Problem:** When a model's parametric knowledge conflicts with context provided in the prompt, it may switch answers — but does its CoT honestly attribute the switch to the context, or hide it? There is no compact benchmark probing CoT honesty under deliberate knowledge conflicts.

**Direction:** Take questions the model answers correctly from parametric knowledge, then inject context asserting a different answer. For items where the model switches, check whether the CoT explicitly cites the injected context as the reason. Report the rate of 'silent switches' (answer changed but context-reliance unverbalized) per open model.

**Why it matters:** Silent context-driven switches mean prompt-injected or retrieved misinformation can change answers without leaving a monitorable trace — a faithfulness and security concern for RAG systems. Behavioral, lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** 'Do Models Know Why They Changed Their Mind? ... CoT Under Knowledge Conflict' (arXiv 2605.27773) and 'Contextual vs Parametric CoT Faithfulness' (2605.24960) study this exact phenomenon. No compact open-model silent-switch benchmark exists.

title: Decoding-Temperature Honesty Surface: Does Sampling Change Truthfulness?
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Decoding-Temperature Honesty Surface: Does Sampling Change Truthfulness?

**Problem:** Honesty and sycophancy evaluations are usually run at a single decoding setting. No benchmark maps how truthfulness, abstention, and sycophancy vary across temperature/top-p for open models, leaving a blind spot in how robust honesty is to deployment-time sampling choices.

**Direction:** Run a fixed honesty/sycophancy probe set (TruthfulQA subset + false-premise items) across a grid of temperatures and top-p values for an open model, averaging over multiple samples. Plot a 'honesty surface' showing how truthful-answer rate and sycophancy rate shift with sampling, and identify settings that maximize dishonesty.

**Why it matters:** Deployers freely tune decoding parameters; if honesty degrades at common high-temperature settings, that's an unmonitored risk. The study needs only repeated sampling of open models — cheap and fully external.

**Relevant context:** Overconfidence and sycophancy benchmarks (SycEval, TruthfulQA) typically fix decoding. Catalogue already covers safety consistency across decoding params for jailbreaks, but not honesty/sycophancy specifically. Sampling effects on truthfulness are under-measured.

title: Quantization Honesty Audit: Do Compressed Models Lie More?
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Quantization Honesty Audit: Do Compressed Models Lie More?

**Problem:** Open models are widely deployed in quantized form (4-bit, 8-bit) for consumer GPUs, but no benchmark measures whether quantization degrades honesty properties — sycophancy resistance, calibration, abstention, CoT faithfulness — relative to the full-precision model.

**Direction:** Take one open model in full precision and in 8-bit/4-bit GPTQ/AWQ variants. Run a fixed honesty battery (sycophancy flip-rate, fabricated-entity confabulation, verbalized calibration) on each and report deltas. Identify which honesty properties are most fragile to quantization.

**Why it matters:** Most real-world open-model deployment uses quantized weights; if quantization quietly worsens honesty, every downstream deployer inherits the risk. This is a counterfactually valuable audit that no lab is incentivized to run on community quantizations, and it fits a single consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Honesty batteries draw on TruthfulQA, SimpleQA, SycEval. Quantization is the standard way participants run models on Colab/Runpod. No existing benchmark isolates quantization's effect on honesty/sycophancy/faithfulness.

title: Honesty-vs-Helpfulness Tension Probe with Forced Tradeoffs
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Honesty-vs-Helpfulness Tension Probe with Forced Tradeoffs

**Problem:** Training tensions between helpfulness and honesty cause instruction-following to override truthfulness, but there's no benchmark that constructs explicit forced-choice items where being helpful requires being dishonest, and measures which a model prioritizes.

**Direction:** Construct prompts where the user explicitly wants a specific (false) conclusion confirmed, or wants help that requires asserting something untrue. Score each open model on whether it (a) honestly refuses/corrects, (b) hedges, or (c) complies dishonestly. Report a helpfulness-over-honesty rate and how it shifts with politeness/insistence of the request.

**Why it matters:** The helpfulness-honesty tradeoff is the root cause of much sycophancy and fabrication; a benchmark that forces the tradeoff cleanly measures a model's honesty 'spine' and is fully promptable on open models.

**Relevant context:** 'When Models Fabricate Credentials' (arXiv 2511.21569): instruction-following overrides honesty. Personas-as-truthfulness (2310.18168) and the honesty open-problems list highlight this tension. No forced-tradeoff honesty-vs-helpfulness benchmark exists.

title: CoT Faithfulness Classifier-Sensitivity Robustness Check
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined honesty/faithfulness (CoT monitoring, sycophancy, or calibration) safety problem with a clear focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# CoT Faithfulness Classifier-Sensitivity Robustness Check

**Problem:** A recent finding is that measured CoT faithfulness depends heavily on which classifier/judge is used to decide whether a CoT 'mentions' a factor. There's no reusable tool that quantifies how much a faithfulness verdict swings across different cheap judges, alerting researchers to fragile measurements.

**Direction:** Take a fixed set of (CoT, factor) pairs and run multiple cheap verbalization judges (keyword match, embedding similarity, small-LLM judge with different prompts). # Faithfulness Under Paraphrase: Does Restating the Question Change the Hidden-Cue Effect?

**Problem:** Counterfactual faithfulness tests include paraphrasing, and prior work found paraphrasing CoT rarely changes answers. But paraphrasing the *prompt* (not the CoT) while keeping a planted bias cue constant is a sharper unfaithfulness probe that is rarely isolated.

**Direction:** Plant a biasing cue (e.g. 'I think the answer is B') and present semantically equivalent paraphrases of the surrounding question. Measure whether the cue's silent influence on the answer is stable across paraphrases and whether acknowledgment changes. Stable hidden influence across paraphrases = robust unfaithfulness.

**Why it matters:** Robustness of hidden-cue influence to surface form tells us whether unfaithfulness is a shallow phrasing artifact or a deep behavioral bias. This sharpens what CoT monitors must contend with. Cheap, training-free, public datasets.

**Relevant context:** Lanham et al. 2023 (paraphrasing intervention); Turpin et al. 2023 biasing-cue setup (github.com/milesaturpin/cot-unfaithfulness); 'CoT Reasoning In The Wild Is Not Always Faithful' (arXiv:2503.08679).

# Quantization-Induced Honesty Regression: Does Compressing a Model Make It More Sycophantic?

**Problem:** Practitioners deploy quantized (4-bit/8-bit) open models for cost. Whether quantization degrades honesty properties — sycophancy resistance, hint-acknowledgment, calibration — separately from raw accuracy is essentially unstudied and a sharp, surprising-if-true failure mode.

**Direction:** Take one open model at full precision and at 8-bit/4-bit quantization (same weights, single GPU). Run identical sycophancy-pressure, hint-injection, and confidence-calibration probes on each. Measure whether honesty metrics regress more (or less) than accuracy under quantization.

**Why it matters:** If the cheap deployment path silently erodes honesty, every cost-conscious deployment (exactly the lab-independent ones) is more dangerous than its accuracy benchmarks suggest. This is a practical, fully reproducible, single-GPU failure investigation with no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** 'On the Impact of Fine-Tuning on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning' (arXiv:2411.15382) shows training changes faithfulness; analogously quantization may shift behavior. SycEval/MASK provide ready-made honesty probes to apply pre/post quantization.

# The 'I Don't Know' Suppression Effect: Does Adding a Persona Reduce Honest Abstention?

**Problem:** Two findings combine into an untested interaction: (1) models under-abstain due to scoring incentives, and (2) expert personas suppress honest self-representation. Whether assigning a confident expert persona specifically reduces honest 'I don't know' rates on hard questions is open.

**Direction:** On hard factual items where abstention is the honest move, compare a neutral assistant prompt vs. a confident-expert persona. Measure abstention rate and confident-wrong rate in each condition across open models, isolating the persona's effect on honest uncertainty disclosure.

**Why it matters:** Persona-driven confidence inflation is a plausible, common, and harmful failure (e.g. an 'expert' chatbot that never says it doesn't know). Quantifying it connects two literatures and is directly useful for safe system-prompt design. Pure prompting.

**Relevant context:** Self-transparency/credential-fabrication results (arXiv:2511.21569); OpenAI hallucination-incentive argument on abstention; I-CALM (arXiv:2604.03904). Anthropic recommended directions flags persona effects.

# Does Sampling Temperature Change Whether the CoT Tells the Truth?

**Problem:** Faithfulness studies typically fix decoding settings. Whether hint-acknowledgment and answer-vs-thinking consistency vary with temperature/top-p is unknown — yet temperature is the easiest knob a deployer turns.

**Direction:** Hold the hint-injection / belief-consistency protocol fixed and sweep temperature and top-p on a small reasoning model. Measure how acknowledgment rate, answer-flip rate, and thinking-answer consistency move with sampling. Identify whether any decoding regime maximizes faithful self-reporting.

**Why it matters:** If faithfulness is decoding-dependent, then reported faithfulness numbers are fragile and monitors should pin decoding. A simple sweep gives an actionable 'most-faithful decoding' recommendation. Single GPU, no training, fully reproducible.

**Relevant context:** Prior covered idea 'Consistency of Safety Across Decoding Parameters' targeted refusal safety; this is distinct — it targets CoT faithfulness/honesty metrics. Builds on Turpin/Lanham faithfulness protocols and the answer-vs-thinking gap (arXiv:2603.26410).

# Verbosity-Reward Echo: Do Models Pad Confident Prose When Honesty Requires Brevity?

**Problem:** RLHF reportedly rewards long, confident answers, biasing models toward verbose certainty over honest hedging. Whether small open chat models exhibit a measurable correlation between answer length and overconfidence (length as a tell for fabrication) is a concrete, testable failure pattern.

**Direction:** On a factual QA set with known answers, measure answer length, expressed confidence, and correctness per item. Test whether longer answers are systematically more confident-yet-wrong (i.e. length predicts unwarranted confidence). Characterize the length-vs-honesty relationship per model.

**Why it matters:** If response length is a cheap proxy for likely fabrication, monitors and users get a free honesty heuristic. It also documents an RLHF side-effect (verbosity bias) in the open models people actually run. No lab data needed.

**Relevant context:** OpenAI/hallucination-incentive analyses note RLHF favors long confident answers over balanced ones; human judges prefer confident responses. SimpleQA/TruthfulQA provide labeled factual items.

# Cross-Layer Refusal Localization: Where in the Network Does Safety Live?

**Problem:** Success state: defenders know which layers carry safety so they can monitor/protect them cheaply. Needed prior result: a per-layer map of where refusal becomes linearly decodable, and whether it matches where attacks first disrupt it.

**Direction:** Train linear refusal probes at every layer of an open model, plot decodability vs depth, then run a prefill/suffix attack and identify the layer where the refusal signal first collapses. Compare 'safety-bearing layer' across 2-3 models. Activation extraction + sklearn only.

**Why it matters:** Gives the cheap-monitoring agenda a principled answer to 'which layer should the probe read?' and connects mechanistic localization to attack dynamics — accessible interpretability-adjacent work needing no training.

**Relevant context:** Arditi et al. (arXiv:2406.11717) localize refusal to a single direction in the residual stream; cheap-probe work (arXiv:2509.14558) reuses internal features but layer choice is under-studied. Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction's propagation across layers.
